en: The Sampaguita, our national flower, is recognizable by its small, star-shaped white blossoms and strong sweet fragrance.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has a distinctive crest of dark brown feathers and measures up to one meter tall.
The Narra, the national tree, is easily identified by its compound leaves and hard, reddish-brown wood used in local furniture.
The Pahiyas Festival in Lucban displays harvested rice grains and colorful kiping on house facades to thank the patron saint.
The T'boli people weave T'nalak cloth using abaca fibers extracted from the stalks of locally grown abaca plants.
The Ifugao carved the Banaue Rice Terraces into steep mountains, creating a massive irrigation system fed by natural rainforests.
The Philippine pearl, our national gem, is a lustrous white or golden pearl harvested from local oysters in the Sulu Sea.
During the Panagbenga Festival in Baguio City, locals celebrate the blooming season by parading floats decorated with thousands of fresh orchid flowers.
Filipinos call the coconut tree the tree of life because almost every physical part of the plant, from fronds to water, is useful.
The Mangyan people use the ancient Surat Mangyan script to carve poetic ambahan verses onto the smooth, cylindrical surfaces of bamboo tubes.
The Tamaraw, the national mammal, is a small, hoofed, horned bovine endemic to the island of Mindoro and distinct from the carabao.
National Scientist Angel Alcala studied coral reefs, observing how marine protected areas in the Philippines allow damaged fish populations to naturally recover.
